chapter.title: Appendix: README-driven with Grill Driven Development (RGDD)
chapter.body_html:
RGDD (README-driven with Grill Driven Development) is a way of developing that I came up with when I used the ideas in this book and pstack on my personal projects.

In RGDD, the developer puts the context the agent reads into the codebase before the code, and develops while the agent reads that context.

!

Context is the set of files, mostly in the repository, that the agent reads again each time it works.
It stays after a conversation ends.

In Chapter 4, I treated the codebase as the agent's memory and wrote the following.

The memory that lets the agent carry forward earlier decisions belongs in the codebase, not in the model.

Besides code, RGDD uses the following documents as context.

  • README. A document that says who uses the software, for what, and how. Usage instructions and a tutorial are examples.
  • GLOSSARY.md. A document that lists domain terms and their definitions, such as what "order" means. A domain term is a word for the business or the things the software deals with.
  • ADR (Architecture Decision Record). A record of a design decision and the reason for it, such as why the team chose a particular database.
  • Coding standards. The rules for how to write code, such as the rules in CODING_STANDARDS.md.
  • Feature Map and verification skill. A verification skill is a project-specific Skill that lets the agent start and operate the app to collect evidence. The Feature Map is a document inside that skill. For each feature of the app, the Feature Map says how to reach the feature and how to verify it (Chapter 36).

Of these, the developer puts the README, GLOSSARY.md, and ADRs in place before the code. The developer has the agent create the Feature Map and the verification skill after the first feature works.

This appendix explains the ideas behind RGDD and how to carry it out.

How this appendix is organized

This appendix covers the following topics.

  • RGDD builds context with README-driven development and /grill-with-docs, then uses it to develop and verify
  • RGDD adds to the context and verifies and updates it in five phases
  • The context keeps growing because each phase reads the previous phase's context and adds to it
  • Context comes first so that the examples the agent reads are right from the start
  • Summary: put the context before the code
!

The context grows means that each piece of work adds terms and decisions to the context files, and that the developer and the agent keep verifying, correcting, and updating the content already there.

RGDD builds context with README-driven development and /grill-with-docs, then uses it to develop and verify

In RGDD, the developer combines README-driven development with Matt Pocock's Skill /grill-with-docs to build context. The developer then uses that context to develop and verify.

!

README-driven development is a way of developing that starts with a README that explains usage to the intended users, then works backward to the implementation and the architecture.

I explain README-driven development in "1. Write the user's view of the app in the README" and /grill-with-docs in "2. Create domain terms and ADRs with /grill-with-docs".

RGDD rests on the idea from Chapter 4, quoted at the start, that the codebase is the agent's memory.

poteto writes the following in the section "Keep agents smart with Feature Maps" of The Complete Guide to pstack Part 1.

Personally, I think your codebase is the ultimate form of memory. Code is a projection of the decision making you and your team have made and represents the source of truth for what's happened and how things actually work.

In the same section, poteto describes the Feature Map this way.

A Feature Map is just a more compact form of that, designed to save tokens.

A Feature Map holds the following.

  • What features exist and what each one does
  • How a user reaches each feature
  • How to operate each feature with the verification skill
  • What you need to see to say that the feature works

RGDD widens what the context holds. The README holds "who uses it, for what, and how", GLOSSARY.md holds "which words to use", and the ADRs hold "why we decided this way".

The table below lists the five kinds of context, what each holds, and who or what creates it.

Context What it holds Created by
README (or a document that plays the README's role) Who uses it, for what, and how The developer writes it
GLOSSARY.md Domain terms, their definitions, and avoided terms /grill-with-docs
ADR (docs/adr/) Important design decisions, with their background and reasons /grill-with-docs
Coding standards (for example, CODING_STANDARDS.md) How to write code The developer decides and writes them for each repository
Feature Map and verification skill The list of features, how a user reaches each one, and how to verify it /create-verification-skill
!
  • Domain term. A word for the business or the things the software deals with, such as "order" and "cancellation" in a food-ordering app.
  • Avoided terms. Other words for the same thing that the team decided not to use (for example, if "order" is the chosen term, "purchase" and "transaction" are avoided terms). In GLOSSARY.md, they go under the term's definition.

The five phases do not create the coding standards. The coding standards are rules the agent follows when it writes code with /poteto-mode. So I leave them out of the five phases in the next section. /poteto-mode is pstack's entry Skill, which routes each request to the right way of working (Chapter 7).

Also, the README does not have to be named README.md.

A specification or another document can play the README's role, as long as it describes usage from the user's side and the other context starts from it.

RGDD adds to the context and verifies and updates it in five phases

The developer carries out RGDD in these five phases.

  1. Write the user's view of the app in the README
  2. Create domain terms and ADRs with /grill-with-docs
  3. Develop with /poteto-mode
  4. Review with /thermos
  5. Verify with /create-verification-skill

Each phase does one of two jobs. It adds to the context, or it verifies what the context holds and corrects or updates it.

For each phase below, I explain what it creates, the tool it uses, and the context it leaves behind.

1. Write the user's view of the app in the README

  • What it creates. A README that gives usage instructions and a tutorial from the point of view of the app's user. It does not cover the implementation yet.

  • Tool. In RGDD, the developer writes the README by hand, without a Skill, a CLI, or any other tool. Key point 5 (write the usage first) of Chapter 38 showed a different approach, in which the agent writes the README.

    Before the implementation, the human has the agent write the usage in a README or a tutorial, and has it work backward from that usage to the API and the internals.

  • Context it leaves. Context about how people use the app, such as "who uses it, for what, and how." The other context starts from it.

Example: a README for a food-ordering app

The README describes only what the user sees, not the implementation.

# Order Ahead

An app for ordering food from nearby restaurants on your smartphone.

## What you can do

- Choose dishes from the menu and place an order
- Check the status of an order (received, cooking, ready for pickup)
- Cancel an order before you pick it up

## How to use it

1. Open the app and choose a restaurant
2. Choose dishes from the menu and tap "Place order"
3. When the status changes to "Ready for pickup," pick up the order at the restaurant

RGDD puts this phase first to prepare the material that /grill-with-docs asks questions about in the next phase.

When the README describes usage from the user's side, /grill-with-docs can ask concrete questions about the vague parts of that usage. The developer can then give concrete answers.

For example, the README above says "Cancel an order before you pick it up." From this, /grill-with-docs can ask about something the README leaves open, such as "Can the customer cancel an order that is already cooking?"

2. Create domain terms and ADRs with /grill-with-docs

  • What it creates. A GLOSSARY.md that lists the domain terms, and ADRs that record design decisions.
  • Tool. Matt Pocock's /grill-with-docs. The agent does not pick this Skill on its own, so the developer starts it by name.
  • Context it leaves. Background knowledge, such as domain terms and their definitions (GLOSSARY.md), and past decisions, such as design decisions and their reasons (ADRs).

/grill-with-docs is a Skill that asks the developer question after question to settle a plan or a design, and creates ADRs and a glossary (GLOSSARY.md) along the way.

/grill-with-docs calls these two Skills as part of its steps.

  • /grilling. It asks the developer question after question about the plan or the design and settles what needs a decision.
  • /domain-modeling. It points out conflicting terms and vague wording, and writes each settled term to GLOSSARY.md right away. It offers to record a decision as an ADR only when all three of these are true.
    • Hard to reverse
    • Surprising without context
    • The result of a real trade-off

The following example uses the food-ordering app to explain what each of the three conditions for an ADR means.

Example: the three conditions for an ADR

The "Meaning" column quotes the section "When to offer an ADR" in ADR-FORMAT.md of /domain-modeling. I wrote the "Example" column for this book. It applies each condition to one decision about the food-ordering app, the README example in phase 1: "store each restaurant's order data in a separate database."

Condition Meaning (ADR-FORMAT.md) Example
Hard to reverse The cost of changing your mind later is meaningful To merge into one database later, you have to move every restaurant's data
Surprising without context A future reader will look at the code and wonder "why on earth did they do it this way?" The data is all order data, yet each restaurant stores it in a different place
The result of a real trade-off There were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons Compared with one shared database, separate databases keep a failure confined to one restaurant

A decision that misses even one of these conditions does not become an ADR.

For example, the decision "list orders newest first" is easy to reverse, and nobody will wonder why, so it does not become an ADR. ADR-FORMAT.md gives the reason as follows.

If a decision is easy to reverse, skip it: you'll just reverse it. If it's not surprising, nobody will wonder why. If there was no real alternative, there's nothing to record beyond "we did the obvious thing."

/grilling orders the decisions so that each comes after the decisions it depends on. It then asks, in one round, all the questions the developer can answer now. The following example shows how /grilling proceeds.

Example: how /grilling asks its questions

/grilling arranges the decisions as a design tree. Each branch is a decision that becomes possible only after its parent decision is made.

For Order Ahead, the README example in phase 1, the tree of decisions looks like this. I made this example for this book.

For example, Q3, "how to show the cancellation window to customers," has no answer until Q1, "the cancellation window," is decided. The display depends on whether the window is "only while received" or "until pickup." In the same way, Q4, "how to tell customers who have not allowed notifications," comes up only after Q2 decides "announce it with a push notification."

/grilling asks the questions in this tree over several rounds. Each round contains only questions whose parent decisions are all settled. The skill calls this set of questions the frontier and describes it as follows.

The frontier is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled: the questions you can ask now without guessing at answers you haven't heard yet.

In the tree above, the first round is Q1 and Q2, which need no parent decision. The agent asks Q1 and Q2 at once, each with a number and a recommended answer.

When the developer answers Q1 and Q2, Q3 and Q4 become answerable. The agent asks Q3 and Q4 as the second round.

An example of the first round

This is the first round of the tree above (Q1 and Q2), written in the format that the SKILL.md of /grilling shows: number each question and add a recommended answer.

❓ **Q1** - **Cancellation window**: The README says "Cancel an order before you pick it up." Can the customer cancel an order that is already cooking?

➡️ Allow cancellation only for orders in "received" status (food that is already cooking would go to waste)

---

❓ **Q2** - **How to announce ready for pickup**: How do we tell the customer that the status has changed to "ready for pickup"?

➡️ Send a push notification from the app

When the developer answers Q1 with "received only," the definition of the term "cancellation" is settled. /domain-modeling then writes that definition to GLOSSARY.md.

In this phase, the agent can write the domain terms it settles with the developer to a file, GLOSSARY.md, instead of leaving them only in the conversation.

Terms decided in a conversation do not carry over to the next agent once the conversation ends.

Terms written to GLOSSARY.md, on the other hand, are there for the next agent to read.

While the developer and the agent settle the design with /grill-with-docs, the agent also compares the developer's words with the term definitions in GLOSSARY.md.

When the developer uses wording that conflicts with a definition, the agent points out the conflict immediately. The section "Challenge against the glossary" in the SKILL.md of /domain-modeling sets this rule. In the quote, "the user" is the person who uses the Skill, which in RGDD is the developer.

When the user uses a term that conflicts with the existing language in GLOSSARY.md, call it out immediately.

The _Avoid_ list in GLOSSARY.md is what helps the agent spot a conflict. The section "Rules" of the GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md of /domain-modeling says that when several words name the same thing, you pick the best one as the term and list the others as avoided terms.

When multiple words exist for the same concept, pick the best one and list the others under _Avoid_.

For example, suppose GLOSSARY.md defines "order" and lists "purchase" as an avoided term. This example comes from GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md.

When the developer says "purchase," the agent points it out as wording that conflicts with the definition.

The GLOSSARY.md and the ADRs that this phase creates are short documents like the following.

Example: GLOSSARY.md

It follows the format that GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md of /domain-modeling shows. Each term gets a short definition and its avoided terms.

# Ordering

Covers a customer ordering food from a restaurant, through pickup.

## Language

**Order**:
A request for food that a customer places with a restaurant.
_Avoid_: purchase, transaction

**Cancellation**:
A customer calling off an order that is in "received" status. An order that is cooking cannot be cancelled.
_Avoid_: withdrawal
Example: an ADR (docs/adr/0001-separate-database-per-store.md)

It follows the format that ADR-FORMAT.md of /domain-modeling shows. An ADR is a short document that says what was decided and why. One paragraph is enough.

# Store order data in a separate database for each restaurant

We store each restaurant's order data in its own database, so that a failure at one restaurant does not affect orders at the others. We also considered a single shared database, but rejected it because a failure there would spread to every restaurant.

This ADR records the decision that the table in the collapsible section "Example: the three conditions for an ADR" checked against the three conditions.

3. Develop with /poteto-mode

  • What it creates. The code.
  • Tool. The developer uses /poteto-mode for development (Chapter 7). When the developer wants to know how the code works or how it got this way, the developer uses these Skills (Chapter 22).
    • /how looks into how something works
    • /why looks into the reasons behind a design
    • /recall gathers the history of recent work from chat history and other sources
  • Context it leaves. The code itself, and PRs. The agent creates the PR in the last step of a Playbook, such as the one for adding a feature or fixing a bug. A Playbook is a step-by-step procedure for one kind of work (Chapter 8).

In the development phase, the agent writes code while it reads the context that earlier phases created, and the coding standards if the developer has prepared them.

For light or routine work, such as feedback, QA, and bug fixes, I have Grok Bot start Cloud Agents to do the work. Grok Bot is an AI bot app (Chapter 5). Cloud Agents is the Cursor feature that runs agents in Cursor's cloud.

Like poteto, I do not have Grok Bot do the work itself. I have it start Cloud Agents.

In Chapter 36, I described how poteto works as follows.

When he sends the request from a Grok Bot, poteto does not have the bot do the work itself. He asks the bot to start an agent in Cloud Agents, a Cursor feature that runs agents in Cursor's cloud.

The README, GLOSSARY.md, ADRs, and coding standards live in the repository, so every agent that works on the repository can read them, Cloud Agents included.

The ADRs from phase 2 also help during development, when the developer asks /why for the reason behind a decision.

/why has a file for each kind of source it searches, and each file says how to search that source.

The file for source control history includes a step that looks for ADRs in docs/adr/ and similar places.

So if an ADR states the reason, /why can base its answer on that ADR.

Even for a decision without an ADR, /why puts together a reason. It searches source control history, tickets, chat, and other sources in parallel, and uses the clues left there. For tickets and chat, it searches the ones connected through MCP, the mechanism that connects the agent to external tools and data.

If /why still finds no clues, it reports what it searched and says that the reason is Unknown.

4. Review with /thermos

  • What it creates. A list of review findings.
  • Tool. The Cursor plugin /thermos.
  • Context it leaves. The code after the agent fixes the findings. The steps of /thermos end when it merges the findings into one list. They do not include code fixes.

/thermos has two subagents audit the diff of the code the agent wrote in phase 3. The two subagents work in parallel.

!

A subagent is a separate agent that does work that the main agent, the agent that runs /thermos, hands off.

The two audits are as follows.

  • A security and correctness audit, for problems such as bugs, changes that break existing features, and security holes
  • A strict code quality audit, for problems such as code that is hard to maintain, bloated files, and unneeded abstractions

When both audits finish, /thermos removes duplicates and merges the results into one list.

When both subagents point out the same problem, /thermos treats that finding as more important.

RGDD has this phase to remove ad hoc workarounds and hard-to-maintain structures before anyone merges them and they stay in the code. A workaround is code that avoids a problem for the moment without fixing its cause. If a workaround stays in the code, the next agent takes it for a correct implementation example and copies it.

Chapter 4 puts it this way.

You should not keep everything as memory. If you keep an ad hoc workaround, the next agent takes it for a correct implementation and copies it. The copy then produces the next copy, and an undesirable pattern spreads without anyone noticing.

5. Verify with /create-verification-skill

  • What it creates. A project-specific verification skill that includes a small CLI that operates the app and a Feature Map (Chapter 36).
  • Tool. pstack's /create-verification-skill, and /maintain-verification-skill, which keeps the verification skill and the Feature Map up to date (Chapter 26).
  • Context it leaves. Context about what features exist, how a user reaches each one, and how to verify it.

/create-verification-skill builds the Feature Map from an index, features/README.md, and one file per feature.

The index links to each feature file. Each feature file describes these four things from the user's point of view.

  • What the feature is
  • How to reach it
  • How to operate it with the verification skill's CLI
  • What you need to see to say that it works
Example: a feature file (an excerpt from pstack's sample)

This is the file for the "Create a note" feature of a notes app, one of the samples in references/feature-map-example/ of /create-verification-skill, with some parts left out.

# Create a note

Create note lets a user save a titled note from the browser or CLI, cancel an unfinished draft, and confirm the saved note from a second user-facing view.

## Sub-features

- `create-open` opens a blank editor from each browser entry point.
- `create-save` persists a title and body.

## How to get to it (user POV)

- Choose the `New note` button in the browser toolbar.
- Press `n` in the browser while focus is outside an editable field.
- Run `notes create --title <title> --body <body>` in a terminal.

## Driving it with control-notes

- **Open editor.** Choose `New note`. Run `control-notes browser click --role button --name "New note"`. A form named `Note editor` appears with focus in the `Title` textbox.
- **Enter content.** Type the title and body. Run `control-notes browser fill --role textbox --name "Title" --value "Release checklist"` and `control-notes browser fill --role textbox --name "Body" --value "Tag and publish"`. The `Save note` button becomes enabled.
- **Save note.** Choose `Save note`. Run `control-notes browser click --role button --name "Save note"`. A status named `Note saved` appears and the heading reads `Release checklist`.

## Gotchas

- Pressing `n` while a textbox has focus types the character instead of opening a new editor.

The description paragraph under the title is "what the feature is." How to get to it (user POV) is "how to reach it." Driving it with control-notes covers both "how to operate it" and "what you need to see to say that it works."

control-notes is the CLI that this sample verification skill uses to operate the app. Sub-features lists the smaller features, one per line, each with a short ID. Gotchas lists traps that waste verification work or make the results invalid. Every feature file uses the same four English headings in the same order.

The Feature Map index, features/README.md, shares its name with the README from phase 1, but it has a different role.

The README from phase 1 is a document in which the developer describes how to use something that is not built yet.

The Feature Map's features/README.md, on the other hand, is an index of the finished app that the agent creates by following the steps of /create-verification-skill.

The Complete Guide to pstack Part 1 calls the verification skill the most important skill and lists it as the first thing to build (Chapter 36). RGDD takes the same view.

When you build an app from scratch, though, there is no app to run and verify yet, so RGDD puts this phase last.

!

If you already have an app, this book strongly recommends that you create a verification skill and a Feature Map with /create-verification-skill.

The SKILL.md of /create-verification-skill also assumes a working app. If the app cannot build or start as it is, this SKILL.md tells the agent to fix the build or startup before it creates the verification skill, or to report the state accurately. The section "1. Interview the repo, not the user" has this rule.

So in RGDD, once the first feature works, the developer runs /create-verification-skill and has the agent create the verification skill.

From then on, the agent uses that verification skill to verify its changes in every task. The developer keeps the verification skill and the Feature Map up to date with /maintain-verification-skill.

As The Complete Guide to pstack Part 1 recommends, I run /maintain-verification-skill at least once a day. I hand off the runs to a maintainer bot in Grok Bot.

As Part 1 also recommends, I had Dr Eggbot (Chapter 36) build this bot.

I recommend running /maintain-verification-skill at least once a day to ensure that your agents always have the latest details on controlling your app.

The context keeps growing because each phase reads the previous phase's context and adds to it

The context keeps growing because each RGDD phase reads the context the previous phase left, then adds to the context, or verifies what the context holds and corrects or updates it.

Phase What it reads What it adds to the context, or verifies and corrects or updates
1. README Nothing Who uses it, for what, and how
2. /grill-with-docs README Terms and decisions (ADRs)
3. /poteto-mode README, GLOSSARY.md, ADRs, coding standards Code and PRs
4. /thermos The diff of the code written in phase 3 Problems in the diff (the agent fixes them before they stay in the code)
5. /create-verification-skill The working app The Feature Map and how to verify each feature

As development goes on, the developer and the agent keep adding to the context and verifying, correcting, and updating it, as follows.

  • When a new term or decision comes up. The developer settles the design again with /grill-with-docs. The agent adds the term to GLOSSARY.md and offers an ADR for any decision that meets all three of these.
    • Hard to reverse
    • Surprising without context
    • The result of a real trade-off
  • When a review finds a problem in the diff. The agent fixes the /thermos findings before anyone merges the code.
  • When features are added. The developer runs /maintain-verification-skill. If it finds something to fix, such as a feature missing from the Feature Map, the agent puts the fixes into one PR.

The main aim of working this way is to keep leaving the right context for the agent, past context included.

This aim comes from the "gardener" idea in Chapter 4. Chapter 4 described the work to keep the codebase as memory this way.

The talk compares the work of keeping this environment in shape to a gardener's work. A garden does not stay healthy if you only add plants. You have to keep removing unneeded branches and weeds and keep maintaining it so that the plants you want can grow.

The same is true of a codebase. You have to keep removing old workarounds and bad implementation examples, in addition to adding knowledge.

In RGDD, the developer and the agent do this gardener's work on the README, GLOSSARY.md, ADRs, and the Feature Map, in addition to the code.

  • Add. Add newly settled terms and decisions to GLOSSARY.md and the ADRs. In the garden, this step is the planting of what you want to grow.
  • Verify, then correct or update. Check term definitions that have gone stale and a Feature Map that no longer matches the app, and fix them. In the garden, this step is the removal of unneeded branches and weeds.

ADRs do most of the work to keep past context. An ADR records a decision and its reason. Even if you change the decision later, the next agent can read why the team first decided the earlier way.

The ADR-FORMAT.md of /domain-modeling allows a Status at the top of an ADR, for when the team revisits a decision. There are four statuses: proposed, accepted, deprecated, and superseded by ADR-NNNN.

Because a "superseded by" status exists, this book reads the format to mean that when you change a decision, you keep the old ADR and add a new one.

Example: ADRs after a decision changes

This example assumes that the decision in ADR 0001, the ADR example from phase 2, changes later. The statuses follow the four that ADR-FORMAT.md lists.

Keep the old ADR and change only its status to "superseded by 0002."

docs/adr/0001-separate-database-per-store.md
---
status: superseded by ADR-0002
---

# Store order data in a separate database for each restaurant

We store each restaurant's order data in its own database, so that a failure at one restaurant does not affect orders at the others. We also considered a single shared database, but rejected it because a failure there would spread to every restaurant.

The new ADR says what was decided again, and why.

docs/adr/0002-single-database-for-orders.md
---
status: accepted
---

# Store all order data in one database

We now have more than 300 restaurants and can no longer operate a database for each one, so we move all order data into one database. To limit the problem 0001 tried to avoid, a failure spreading to every restaurant, we replicate the database to several locations.

The next agent learns the current decision from 0002, and learns from 0001 why each restaurant used to have its own database.

Context comes first so that the examples the agent reads are right from the start

When you keep context, you can pass what you decided on to the next agent.

You put that context in place before the code so that the examples the agent reads are right from the start.

In this book, I take the view that if you start with the code, the opposite of RGDD, the only way to create context is to derive it from the code afterward.

Then the context may keep even ad hoc workarounds that got into the code, as if they were correct.

A workaround left in the code becomes an example for the next agent (phase 4).

Summary: put the context before the code

  • What is RGDD? A way of developing in which you put the README, GLOSSARY.md, and ADRs in place before the code, and develop while the agent reads them.
  • In what order does it proceed? In five phases: README, then /grill-with-docs, then /poteto-mode, then /thermos, then /create-verification-skill.
  • Why does the context keep growing? Because every phase either adds to the context or verifies it and corrects or updates it.
  • Why does the context come first? So that the examples the agent reads are right from the start.

The final "Afterword" gives the book's conclusion and the first step to take after you finish reading.
